title: TypeScript tutorial: types, interfaces, generics and narrowing — cv.cm
description: Learn TypeScript in one page: install tsc and run Hello world, basic types, interfaces, union types, narrowing, generics, error handling and a full example.
answer: TypeScript is JavaScript with static types. You add type annotations such as `let count: number = 0`, and the compiler `tsc` checks them before turning the code into plain JavaScript that runs in any browser or in Node.js. The key ideas are basic types, interfaces and type aliases for object shapes, union types with narrowing, and generics for reusable code. Types are erased at runtime.

sections.h: What TypeScript is and what it is used for
body: TypeScript is an open-source language developed by Microsoft and first released in 2012. Every valid JavaScript program is also valid TypeScript, so you can adopt it file by file. The type checker catches mistakes such as misspelled properties or a missing `null` check while you type, and editors use the types for autocomplete and safe renaming. It is widely used for large front-end apps (Angular is written in it, and React, Vue and Svelte support it well), Node.js back ends and libraries.
Install Node.js first, then install the compiler in your project with npm. `tsc` compiles `.ts` files to `.js`.

body.code:
npm install --save-dev typescript
npx tsc --init          # creates tsconfig.json
npx tsc hello.ts        # writes hello.js
node hello.js
# Hello, world

body: Recent versions of Node.js, Deno and Bun can also run `.ts` files directly by removing the type annotations. They do not type-check, so still run `npx tsc --noEmit` to find type errors.
You rarely need to write every type. When you initialize a variable, TypeScript infers its type: `let n = 5` is a `number`. Annotate function parameters and public APIs.

rows: Any value, must be checked before use

body: The second line is a deliberate compile error, shown to illustrate what the checker reports.

Control flow (`if`, `for`, `while`, `switch`) is exactly the same as in JavaScript. What TypeScript adds is narrowing: after a check such as `typeof x === "string"`, the compiler knows the more specific type inside that branch.
`string | number` is a union type: the value is one of the listed types. Optional parameters are written `name?: string`, and their type includes `undefined`.
Describe the shape of objects with an `interface` or a `type` alias. TypeScript checks structure, not names: any object with the right properties fits.

sections.h: Signature features: generics and discriminated unions
body: Generics let one function or type work with many types while keeping them connected. A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a literal field, so a `switch` on that field narrows the type, and the compiler can check that every case is handled.

Built-in utility types build new types from old ones: `Partial<User>` makes every property optional, `Pick<User, "id" | "name">` keeps only some properties, and `Record<string, number>` describes a dictionary.
Errors work as in JavaScript, with `throw` and `try`/`catch`. With the `strict` option on, the caught value has type `unknown`, because any value can be thrown, so check it before use.

sections.h: A small complete program: typed inventory
body: Try changing `qty: 10` to `qty: "10"`: the compiler reports the error before the code ever runs.

body.note: Types do not exist at runtime. A type annotation on data from `JSON.parse` or `fetch` is only a promise you make; validate untrusted input with real checks or a schema library.

ul: Using `any` to silence errors. Prefer `unknown` and narrow it.
Overusing `as` type assertions, which tell the compiler to trust you instead of checking.
Leaving `strict` off in `tsconfig.json`. Turn it on in new projects; it enables `null` checks.
Writing types the compiler can already infer, which adds noise without safety.

body: Read the official TypeScript Handbook, and experiment in the TypeScript Playground on typescriptlang.org, which shows the compiled JavaScript and errors side by side. Then learn `tsconfig.json` options, type declaration files for libraries (`@types/...` packages), and TypeScript with your framework of choice.

faq.q: Is TypeScript a different language from JavaScript?
faq.a: It is a superset of JavaScript: it adds type syntax and a checker, then compiles to plain JavaScript. Runtime behavior is the same as the JavaScript it produces.

faq.q: Should I learn JavaScript before TypeScript?
faq.a: Learn the JavaScript basics first (variables, functions, objects, promises), because TypeScript does not change them. Then add TypeScript; the types are easier to learn once the runtime behavior is familiar.

faq.q: What is the difference between interface and type?
faq.a: Both describe object shapes. Interfaces can be extended and merged by declaring them again; type aliases can also name unions, tuples and other non-object types. For plain object shapes either works.

faq.q: Does TypeScript make my code faster?
faq.a: No. Types are removed during compilation, so the output runs at the same speed as hand-written JavaScript. The benefit is fewer bugs and better tooling.
